card.title: TACTICAL RETREAT
card.text: When a friendly unit is attacked, send it to hand before damage.
card.flavorText: Tactical or strategic retreats were a key feature of German military doctrine, refined during campaigns on the Eastern Front. Facing overwhelming Soviet offensives, German units often executed planned withdrawals to shorten supply lines, regroup, and avoid encirclement. These tactics, known as mobile defense, were most effectively used in 1943 and 1944 after the defeat at Stalingrad. A textbook example came during the Third Battle of Kharkov in 1943. German forces allowed the Soviets to overextend, then struck back with concentrated armored formations. The counterattack, led by Field Marshal Erich von Manstein, encircled and destroyed several Soviet spearheads. This approach, known as the “backhand blow”, aimed to trade ground for time and to bleed the enemy in costly engagements. By using flexible defense and local superiority, German forces were able to restore much of the lost front. While not a path to victory, tactical retreats gave the Wehrmacht time to delay collapse on the Eastern Front.
